title: Personal control of correlated color temperature of light: Effects on thermal comfort, visual comfort, and cognitive performance
research_question: 1) Does personal control of CCT improve thermal comfort by enhancing visual comfort in mild cold? 2) Does personal control of CCT benefit cognitive performance, eye-related symptoms, alertness, pleasure and arousal?

participants.description: 16 participants (8 females taking hormonal contraception, 8 males), healthy, normal chronotype, 18-40 years old, BMI 18.0-27.5 kg/m², living in or near the Netherlands for more than two months.
participants.recruitment: Not explicitly stated, but implies recruitment from Maastricht University area.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Windowless climate chamber at Maastricht University. Personal lighting system with two Hue Aurelle Rectangular Lights (Signify) (one ceiling, one desk). Participants faced desk light and laptop screen. Illuminance fixed at 498.9 ± 5.2 lux at eye level. Thermal conditions: mild cold (17.2 °C ± 0.3 °C air temperature, 17.2 °C ± 0.2 °C mean radiant temperature, 40-48% relative humidity, 0.15-0.26 m/s air speed). Clothing insulation standardized at 0.8 clo. CCT varied between 2700 K and 5700 K in 20 perceptually equal steps.

measures.instrument: Visual analogue scale for 9 body parts

mechanisms: Personal control allows individuals to adjust objective lighting conditions to their personal preferences, leading to improved subjective appraisals.

The psychological effect of having control (perceived control) and the personalization effect of exercising control (having exercised it to tune settings to personal preference) contribute to positive outcomes.
The actual CCT itself has direct physiological and cognitive effects, which can interact with the effects of personal control.
Obtaining preferred conditions may improve performance via affective and motivational pathways (Baron's positive affect theory).
Brightness sensation is positively related to CCT, leading to indirect effects of CCT control on perceived illuminance.
implementation_implications: Deployment of personal control of CCT is generally beneficial for visual appraisals and eye-related symptoms.
Personal control of CCT can sometimes improve alertness and reduce mental demand.

Care needs to be taken when the primary interest is cognitive performance related to mental spatial manipulation, as preferred conditions may not be optimal for all cognitive processes (e.g., rotation task).
Antecedent CCT conditions and adjustable range of light can 'nudge' employees to choose settings more favorable for health, performance, or energy saving.

tables.description: Parameter estimates for the effect of having and exercising control as well as the effect of actual CCT on all outcome measures.
key_stats: Visual comfort: Having and exercising control (p<.001, f²=0.26)
Eye strain: Having and exercising control (p<.001, f²=0.07)
Digital span task: Actual CCT (p=0.018, f²=0.07)
Mental demand: Having and exercising control (p<.001, f²=0.05)
Alertness: Having and exercising control (p<.001, f²=0.02)

limitations: The study only investigated the causal route from visual comfort to thermal comfort, not the opposite direction.
Reference conditions were not rated with low visual comfort; benefits of personal control might be more pronounced in real-life situations with compromised visual comfort.
Participants only had control over CCT at the beginning of Period 2 (first 10 min), potentially underestimating the positive effects of personal control.
The study was not able to distinguish the effects of merely perceiving control from the effects of personalization (exercising control) based on regression models.
The test duration was 70 min; beneficial effects of personal control may accrue over a longer time span.
